title: The Herschels: A New Planet
summary: A music teacher and his sister turned their house in Bath into a telescope factory. One night in 1781 William spotted a 'star' that was really a brand-new planet: Uranus. Then Caroline became a famous comet hunter, and together they built a telescope so big that people could walk through its tube.

sections.heading: The Oboe Player Who Fell for the Stars
paragraphs: Imagine a busy, fashionable city in the west of England in the 1770s. Rich visitors stroll between hot-spring baths, ballrooms and concert halls. The city is Bath, and one of its best-known musicians is a tall, friendly man from Germany named William Herschel. He teaches dozens of pupils, writes music, conducts choirs and plays the organ every Sunday. Nobody in the concert crowd would guess that he will soon change astronomy forever.

William was born Friedrich Wilhelm Herschel on 15 November 1738 in Hanover, a German state whose ruler was also, at that time, the King of Great Britain. His father was an oboe player in the Hanoverian army band, and William and his brother Jakob followed him into military music. In 1757, during the Seven Years' War, the French army defeated Hanover's forces at the Battle of Hastenbeck. Teenage William, aged 19, decided army life was not for him. He slipped away to England, changed his name to the English-sounding William, and began scraping a living as a musician.

For about ten years he moved around northern England, copying music, teaching, leading small orchestras and composing. He was very good at it. Over his life he wrote 24 symphonies, many concertos and a lot of church music, and some of it is still performed and recorded today. In 1766 he won the job of organist at the brand-new Octagon Chapel in Bath, and he played his first concert there on 1 January 1767.

Music and mathematics are close cousins. Herschel wanted to understand the science of harmony, so he read a book on the mathematics of music by a Cambridge professor named Robert Smith. Smith had also written a famous textbook called A Compleat System of Opticks, all about lenses, mirrors and telescopes. Herschel picked it up, and then a popular astronomy book by the Scottish writer James Ferguson. By 1773, when he was in his mid-thirties, he was hooked. He did not just want to read about the sky. He wanted to see it.

There was one problem. Good telescopes were expensive, and the ones he could rent or buy were small. Long refractors of the kind you met in part 6 were clumsy, and the achromatic lenses of part 8 could only be made in small sizes. So Herschel made a bold decision that would shape the rest of his life. He would build reflecting telescopes, the mirror type invented by Newton, and he would make the mirrors himself.

sections.heading: A House Turned into a Mirror Factory
paragraphs: A telescope mirror of the 1770s was not glass. It was a disc of speculum metal, a hard, brittle mixture of mostly copper and tin that could be polished until it shone like silver. To make one, you first had to melt the metal and pour it into a mould to make a rough disc called a blank. Then came the long part: grinding the face into a shallow curve with gritty powders, and then polishing it, hour after hour, until it was smooth and had exactly the right shape. A curve that is wrong by even a tiny fraction of the thickness of a hair can turn stars into fuzzy blobs.

Herschel turned his home into a workshop. His younger brother Alexander, a clever mechanic, built a lathe in one of the bedrooms and made eyepieces and metal parts. Tubes and stands were built in the drawing room. The smell of hot metal and the grinding noise filled the house. Herschel's records show that he made hundreds of mirrors over his lifetime, more than 400 by some counts, from about 6 inches up to 48 inches across, and at least 60 complete telescopes.

Polishing could not be stopped halfway, because if you lifted your hands the shape could be spoiled. So Herschel sometimes polished for up to 16 hours at a stretch. His sister Caroline later remembered feeding him bites of food while he worked, and reading aloud to him, from books like Don Quixote and the Arabian Nights, to help the hours pass. It sounds funny, but it was also exhausting and serious work.

Casting the metal was the most dangerous step. Herschel later tried to cast a very large mirror in the basement of one of their Bath houses, using a mould partly made from horse manure, which was a known trick for making moulds that could stand the heat. Caroline described how the molten metal leaked out across the floor and made the stone flagstones crack and fly apart, while everyone ran for safety. Nobody was badly hurt, but the mirror was ruined. Making telescopes was not a quiet hobby.

All this effort paid off. Herschel's mirrors were famous for being some of the best in the world. He used them in Newtonian telescopes, where a small flat mirror near the top of the tube sends the light out to an eyepiece on the side. One of his favourites was a reflector with a mirror about 6.2 inches across and a tube about 7 feet long. With it he could use very high magnifications and still get sharp images, because the mirror's shape was so good.

sections.heading: Caroline Comes to Bath
paragraphs: Caroline Lucretia Herschel was born in Hanover on 16 March 1750, the second youngest of the Herschel children. When she was about 10, she caught typhus, a dangerous fever. She survived, but the illness stunted her growth. As an adult she stood only about 4 feet 3 inches (about 1.30 metres) tall, and she lost some of the sight in one eye. Her mother expected her to stay at home as an unpaid housekeeper for the rest of her life and saw little point in educating her.

William had other ideas. In August 1772 he came back to Hanover and took Caroline, then 22, to live with him in Bath. The plan was that she would keep house for him and train as a singer for his concerts. She practised hard, took lessons two or three times a day, and became a skilled soprano. In April 1778 she was the main soloist in a performance of Handel's Messiah in Birmingham, and she was offered more singing work.

But the house was slowly filling up with telescopes, and Caroline was pulled into the new passion too. At first she helped by grinding, copying, fetching and writing down William's observations as he called them out in the dark. She learned mathematics, especially the sums needed to turn telescope readings into star positions, often teaching herself at the breakfast table. She would later say, a little sadly, that she had become a tool that her brother had trained. Yet she was far more than a tool, as we will see.

Picture the scene on a clear night. William stands at the eyepiece in the garden, wrapped against the cold. Caroline sits at a desk near an open window with a candle shaded from the telescope, a clock and a big record book. William calls out what he sees and where, and Caroline writes it down, notes the exact time and later turns it all into neat, usable tables. Without that partnership, many of William's discoveries would never have been recorded properly.

sections.heading: 13 March 1781: The Star That Wasn't
paragraphs: By 1781 the Herschels were living at 19 New King Street in Bath, a narrow stone townhouse that still stands today as the Herschel Museum of Astronomy. William had set himself an enormous task. He was going to examine every star in the sky down to a certain faintness, one by one, looking especially for double stars, pairs of stars that sit very close together. It was patient, careful, repetitive work, exactly the kind of work that turns up surprises.

On the night of Tuesday 13 March 1781, he was working in the garden with his 6.2-inch homemade reflector, sweeping through the stars near the border of the constellations Taurus and Gemini. One object caught his eye. To most observers it would have looked like any other faint star. But to Herschel, whose telescope was unusually sharp, it did not look like a tiny point. It looked like a little disc.

Here is why that mattered. Stars are so far away that even through a big telescope they stay as points of light; turning up the magnification does not make them look wider. Planets and comets are much closer, so they show a real size. Herschel switched to higher magnifications, hundreds of times, and the object grew larger, while the stars around it did not. Over the following nights, he saw that it had moved slightly against the background stars. Something nearby was travelling across the sky.

What was it? Herschel's first guess was a comet, because new moving objects almost always were comets. In his journal he wrote that it was either a 'nebulous star' or perhaps a comet, and when he reported it to the Royal Society on 26 April 1781, he called it a comet. Nobody had discovered a new planet in all of recorded history. The five planets you can see with your eyes, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, had been known since ancient times. The idea that a sixth one beyond Saturn could be waiting out there just did not occur to most people.

Astronomers across Europe began to track the new object. But it did not behave like a comet. It had no tail and no fuzzy head, and it moved slowly. When mathematicians tried to work out its path, they found it went around the Sun in a nearly circular orbit far beyond Saturn, not on the long stretched-out path of a comet. The Swedish-born astronomer Anders Johan Lexell, working in Russia, was the first to calculate such an orbit, and the German astronomer Johann Bode also concluded that it must be a planet. By 1783 Herschel himself agreed. A music teacher with a homemade telescope had found the first planet ever discovered with a telescope.

It turned out that others had actually seen it before, without realising. The first Astronomer Royal, John Flamsteed, had recorded it in 1690 and listed it as a star called 34 Tauri. The French astronomer Pierre Charles Le Monnier noted it many times between 1750 and 1769. They had all thought it was a star. Herschel was the one who looked carefully enough, with a good enough telescope, to see that it was different.

The discovery doubled the size of the known solar system in one go. Saturn sits about 9.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth does. The new planet sits about 19 to 20 times farther, around 3 billion kilometres away, and takes about 84 years to go around the Sun once. That means someone born on the day of its discovery would have had to live to 84 to see it return to the same place in the sky.

sections.heading: George's Star, or Uranus?
paragraphs: A new planet needed a name. Herschel, living in England and hoping for royal support, suggested Georgium Sidus, Latin for George's Star, after King George III. To British ears that made sense. To astronomers in the rest of Europe, naming a planet after a British king sounded strange. The French astronomer Jérôme Lalande suggested calling it Herschel, and other people proposed names such as Neptune and Minerva.

In 1782 Johann Bode suggested Uranus, after the ancient Greek god of the sky. His reasoning was neat: Saturn was the father of Jupiter in the old myths, and Uranus was the father of Saturn, so the new planet beyond Saturn should be named for him. Most of Europe gradually adopted Uranus. Britain held on to the Georgian name for decades. The last holdout, the British Nautical Almanac Office, only switched to Uranus in 1850, long after both Herschel and the king had died.

The name argument did not hurt Herschel at all. In 1781 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and awarded its Copley Medal, the society's top prize. In 1782 he was invited to show his telescope to King George III at Windsor. The king was impressed and made him the King's Astronomer, with a salary of 200 pounds a year, on the condition that he live near Windsor Castle so the royal family could look through his telescopes. (This is a different job from the Astronomer Royal at Greenwich, whom you will meet in part 10.)

Two hundred pounds was less than Herschel had been earning as a busy musician, but it freed him to do astronomy full time. In August 1782 the family moved to Datchet, near Windsor, and in 1786 they settled in a house at Slough that became known as Observatory House. To boost their income, William built and sold telescopes to customers around Europe, including royalty and observatories. He gave up his music career, and Caroline, rather unhappily at first, gave up her singing career too.

sections.heading: Caroline the Comet Hunter
paragraphs: William gave Caroline her own small telescope and asked her to 'sweep' the sky, slowly moving the telescope back and forth to look for nebulae, faint fuzzy patches of light, and for comets. She began keeping her own observing record book on 28 August 1782. At first she found it lonely and dull. Then she started making discoveries.

On 26 February 1783 she found a nebula that was not in the famous list of fuzzy objects published by the French comet hunter Charles Messier. That same year she independently found a small companion galaxy of the great Andromeda Galaxy, now known as M110. Of course, nobody yet knew that these fuzzy patches could be whole galaxies. That discovery was still 140 years away.

On the night of 1 August 1786, while William was away in Germany delivering a telescope, Caroline spotted a fuzzy object that moved. It was a comet, and she became one of the very first women ever credited with discovering one. She wrote careful letters announcing it to leading astronomers, the news spread quickly, and visitors came to Slough to see the famous lady comet hunter. Between 1786 and 1797 she discovered eight comets in all. In 1795 she also found a comet that turned out to be a return of one seen before, now known as Comet Encke. One comet still carries her name today: 35P/Herschel-Rigollet, which goes around the Sun only about once every century and a half.

In 1787 King George III granted Caroline a salary of 50 pounds a year as her brother's assistant. This made her the first woman in Britain to be paid an official salary for scientific work, and she is often described as the first professional woman astronomer. Fifty pounds was not a fortune, but for Caroline it meant something huge: money of her own, earned by her own skill.

Caroline also did enormous behind-the-scenes work that helped every astronomer. In 1798 the Royal Society published her index and catalogue to John Flamsteed's star observations, in which she found and listed more than 560 stars that Flamsteed had observed but left out of his famous catalogue. She also kept William's huge lists of nebulae in order. Together the Herschels discovered more than 2,400 nebulae and star clusters, and Caroline's careful organising helped lay the groundwork for the New General Catalogue, the list that still gives many galaxies their NGC numbers.

After William died in 1822, Caroline moved back to Hanover. She kept working, finishing a catalogue of the nebulae for her nephew John. In 1828, at the age of 77, she received the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society; no woman would receive it again until 1996. In 1835 she and the Scottish scientist Mary Somerville became the first women made honorary members of the society. At 96 she received a gold medal for science from the King of Prussia. She died in Hanover on 9 January 1848, aged 97. Caroline was not just William's helper. She was a discoverer in her own right.

sections.heading: The Forty-Foot Giant
paragraphs: Herschel knew the lesson you will meet again and again in this Deep Dive: the bigger the mirror, the more light it collects, and the fainter the things you can see. He already had an excellent telescope with a mirror about 18.7 inches across and a tube 20 feet long, which he used for most of his observations. But he dreamed bigger. In 1785 King George III gave him 4,000 pounds to build a monster, plus 200 pounds a year for its upkeep.

The result, finished in 1789 in the garden at Slough, was the famous 40-foot telescope. The name came from the length of its iron tube, about 40 feet (12 metres), wide enough for a grown person to walk through. Its main mirror was about 48 inches (1.2 metres) across. The first mirror, cast in 1785, turned out to be too thin to hold its shape, so a second, thicker mirror was cast in 1788 and finished in 1789. The whole tube sat in a huge wooden frame of poles, ladders and pulleys that could be turned around on a circular track. Workers had to crank it into position.

Herschel did something clever to save light. Instead of using a small second mirror to send the light out to the side, which would have lost some light in the speculum metal, he tilted the main mirror slightly so that the image formed near the top edge of the tube. He then stood or sat in a little platform at the mouth of the tube, high in the air, and looked down into the mirror through an eyepiece, with his back to the sky. This 'front-view' design is now often called a Herschelian telescope. A speaking tube carried his words down to Caroline or another helper writing at the desk below.

Before it was finished, the telescope became a tourist attraction. A well-known story says that King George III, walking through the empty tube with the Archbishop of Canterbury, joked: 'Come, my Lord Bishop, I will show you the way to Heaven!' It may or may not be exactly what he said, but it shows how amazing the giant tube looked to visitors. In February 1787 Herschel had already tested it by lying inside the unfinished tube and holding an eyepiece by hand to look at the Orion Nebula.

In the summer and autumn of 1789, around the time the telescope came into full use, Herschel discovered two new moons of Saturn: Enceladus on 28 August 1789 and Mimas on 17 September 1789. Earlier, on 11 January 1787, using his 20-foot telescope, he had found the two largest moons of Uranus, now called Titania and Oberon. Historians note that he was using several telescopes at that time, so it is not completely certain which ones deserve the credit for the Saturn moons.

The giant had problems. Its speculum mirror tarnished quickly in the damp English air and had to be taken out and repolished often, which was a heavy, risky job. It took a long time to set up, and English nights are often cloudy, so it was used less than its builder had hoped. Herschel's smaller 20-foot telescope did more of the everyday science.

Still, the 40-foot was the largest telescope in the world for about 50 years. In 1839, its wooden frame was rotting, and William's son John took it down for safety. Around New Year 1840, the Herschel family gathered inside the old tube, now lying on the ground, and sang a song written for the occasion. A section of the tube survives at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, and the first, too-thin mirror is kept at the Science Museum in London.

sections.heading: Mapping the Milky Way and Feeling Invisible Light
paragraphs: Herschel wanted to know more than what was in the sky. He wanted to know the shape of everything. In the 1780s he invented a method called star gauging. He pointed his 20-foot telescope at hundreds of small patches spread across the sky and counted how many stars he could see in each. His idea was simple: if you see lots of stars in one direction, the starry system must stretch farther that way; if you see only a few, its edge must be close.

From these counts, published in 1785, he drew the first map of the shape of the Milky Way, based on real measurements. It came out as a flattened, ragged disc, a bit like a grindstone or a thick pancake, much wider than it is thick. That basic idea, that we live in a flat disc of stars, is correct. But his map put the Sun near the middle, which turned out to be wrong. Herschel did not know that clouds of dark dust between the stars block the light of distant stars, so he could not see the true size of the galaxy or where its center lay. That puzzle would be solved in the twentieth century.

He also found that many double stars are not just two stars that happen to line up by chance. By watching some pairs for more than 20 years, he showed in 1803 that they slowly go around each other. That proved the same gravity that holds the solar system together also works among distant stars, a big step in showing that the laws of physics are the same everywhere. He listed more than 800 double and multiple stars.

Then, in 1800, came one of his most surprising discoveries, and it did not even need a telescope. Herschel was testing coloured filters for looking at the Sun safely, and he noticed that some colours felt warmer than others. So he set up an experiment. He used a glass prism to spread sunlight into a rainbow spectrum and placed thermometers with blackened bulbs in the different colours. He kept other thermometers nearby, out of the light, to show the normal room temperature for comparison.

The temperature rose from violet toward red, which already surprised him. Then he moved a thermometer just past the red end, where there was no visible light at all. The temperature there was the highest yet. Some kind of invisible ray was falling on the thermometer and warming it. Herschel called these 'calorific rays', meaning heat rays. Today we call them infrared light. He had discovered, for the first time, that there is light our eyes cannot see. This was a giant clue that the rainbow we see is only a small part of a much bigger family of light, an idea that later parts of this Deep Dive will explore.

Herschel kept observing for many more years. He married a widow named Mary Pitt in 1788, and their only child, John, was born in 1792. In 1816 he received a Hanoverian knighthood, and in 1820 he became the first president of the new Astronomical Society of London, later the Royal Astronomical Society. He died at Observatory House in Slough on 25 August 1822, aged 83. John Herschel became a great astronomer too. In the 1830s he took telescopes to the Cape of Good Hope in southern Africa and surveyed the southern skies, finishing the family project of mapping the whole heavens.

Look at what the Herschels achieved, starting with nothing but music money and a kitchen-table workshop: a new planet, new moons, eight comets, thousands of nebulae, the first measured shape of our galaxy and the first invisible light. And they did it all with telescopes they built themselves. Telescopes were now finding planets. But far from the great observatories, they were also quietly changing life on Earth: on ships, maps, battlefields and backyards.

deepDive: Why did Herschel recognise Uranus when Flamsteed, Le Monnier and others had logged it as an ordinary star? The answer is optics. A star's image in a telescope is set by diffraction and by the blurring of the air, so it never grows into a real disc however much you magnify it. Uranus, by contrast, has a true angular size of only about 3.3 to 4 arcseconds, roughly one five-hundredth of the width of the full Moon. Seeing that as a disc needs a mirror with an excellent figure and high magnification. Herschel's 6.2-inch reflector had a focal length of about 7 feet, and he could use eyepieces giving magnifications of a few hundred times and higher. At low power Uranus looked like a star; at high power it swelled while true stars did not. The second test was motion: over several nights it shifted slightly against the stars. Herschel's careful habit of reporting what he saw honestly, a 'comet or nebulous star', helped others follow it up quickly. Turning a moving dot into a planet needed mathematics. With only a few weeks of observations, the path could fit many orbits. Lexell and others found that a near-circular orbit at about 19 times the Earth-Sun distance fit well, while a comet's long ellipse did not. Remarkably, this distance closely matched a numerical pattern called the Titius-Bode rule, which predicted a planet at about 19.6 times the Earth-Sun distance. That match encouraged astronomers to search for a 'missing planet' between Mars and Jupiter, which led to the discovery of Ceres in 1801. Later, the rule failed badly for Neptune, and today it is seen as a coincidence rather than a law. Historians also discuss how to describe Caroline. Her 1787 royal salary is the earliest known case of a woman in Britain being paid officially for scientific work, but some older accounts presented her only as William's assistant. Her comet discoveries, nebula catalogues and her index to Flamsteed's observations show independent skill. Finally, Herschel's star-gauging model of the galaxy is a good example of reasonable science that was wrong for a hidden reason: he assumed space was transparent. Interstellar dust, only proven in the 1930s, dims distant starlight and fooled his counts into placing the Sun near the center.
funFact: Before he discovered a planet, William Herschel was a busy professional composer, and he wrote 24 symphonies, some of which are still performed today.

check.q: What did William Herschel first think Uranus was when he spotted it in 1781?
